name: Vignola's Corinthian Order

authority.source: Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura, Rome 1562, plates XX-XXV
authority.author: Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola
authority.note: Vignola drew the entablature from Roman fragments, chiefly the round temple in the Forum (the so-called rotunda). Figures from the 1889 Juglaris and Locke translation and Esquie 1930, cross-checked against Ware.

module.name: Semidiameter of the column at the base of the shaft
module.note: Eighteen parts, as for the Ionic and Composite. Twelve is reserved for the Tuscan and Doric.

fluting.profile: semicircular flutes separated by fillets, sometimes cabled to one third of their height

members.name: Plinth of the pedestal base
members.note: Esquie: 'the plinth of its base may be increased from 4 parts to 8 parts' - Vignola's drawn figure is 4, the enlargement is offered as a licence.

members.name: Cyma recta of the pedestal base
Die (dado)
members.note: The die is two squares high: 100 parts high by 50 parts wide (Vignola 1889 plate XX; Esquie plate XXIX). Half-width 25 parts, on which the column base at half-width 25 sits exactly.

members.name: Cyma reversa of the pedestal cap
Plinth
members.note: One third of the base, 1/6 D (Ware). Half-width 25 parts = 18 + Vignola's stated 7 parts of projection, which is also the half-width of the pedestal die.

members.name: Fillet at the foot of the shaft
Shaft proper
members.note: 16 modules 12 parts including the fillets and astragal (Vignola 1889, plate XXIII). 24 semicircular flutes separated by fillets, the flutes sometimes cabled to a third of their height. Diminution 5/6, beginning at one third of the shaft height.

members.name: First (lower) row of eight acanthus leaves
members.enrichment: acanthus, olive-leaf variant in Vignola's own plate
members.note: Bell 2 modules (36 parts), abacus 6 parts; capital 2 modules 6 parts = 42 parts = 1 1/6 D. Ware divides the bell into three equal sixths of a diameter: lower leaves, upper leaves, caulicoli. The bell is cylindrical for its lower 1 module 10 parts and springs from a diameter of 5/6 D.

members.name: Second (upper) row of eight acanthus leaves, set alternately
members.note: Set alternately with the lower row - four facing the sides, four the corners; in plan the two rows make an eight-pointed star.

members.name: Eight caulicoli with helices and angle volutes
members.note: The caulicoli (cabbage stalks) rise from between the second-row leaves; each divides into a large angle volute and a small helix meeting its neighbour under the centre of the abacus, where a rosette or flower sits. Sixteen leaves of a third row sheathe the caulicoli.

members.name: Ovolo of the abacus
members.note: Quarter-round 2 parts high (Vignola 1889, plate XXI). Half-width 36 parts is the horn of the abacus: Vignola gives the plan as a hollow-sided square with diagonals 4 modules long. Ware instead gives the abacus 9/6 D = 54 parts across the flats, which a 4-module diagonal will not quite produce; the disagreement is about a part and a half at the horn.

members.name: First fascia
members.note: Ware: three bands and a large cymatium, the cymatium as high as the first band; the two lower bands take the lower half of the architrave, the third band and the cymatium the upper half. That fixes 6 + 6 + 1.5 of mouldings below and 7.5 + 6 above.

members.name: Frieze
members.enrichment: commonly carved with scrolling foliage in the richest examples

members.name: Astragal at the top of the frieze
members.note: Vignola 1889, plate XXII: 'The frieze is 1 1/2 moduli high, and at the top is ornamented by a fillet and a bead.'

members.name: Cyma reversa of the bed mould
Dentil band
members.note: Dentils 1/6 D high, 1/9 D wide, interdentil 1/18 D, 1/6 D on centres - the same dentil as the Ionic. Four dentils to each modillion: one under every modillion and three between (Ware).

members.name: Modillion band
members.note: Ware: the cornice is divided into five equal parts, the middle fifth being the modillion band. Each modillion is 5/12 D long (15 parts, half the upper diameter of the shaft), 1/5 D high, and as wide as a dentil and two interdentils, i.e. 2/9 D (8 parts); they stand 2/3 D = 24 parts on centres with 4/9 D between, exactly twice their width. One modillion must come over the axis of every column - which is why Vignola's Corinthian intercolumniation is 6 2/3 modules, five modillion spacings.

members.name: Cyma reversa crowning the modillion band
Corona
members.note: The soffit between the modillions is sunk as a caisson with a large rosette in the middle of each.

members.name: Crowning fillet
members.note: Cornice projection 2 modules 2 parts = 38 parts (Vignola 1889, plate XXII); Ware's general rule of projection equal to height would give 36.

invariants.statement: The entablature is one quarter the height of the column, base and capital included. Five modules to twenty.

The pedestal is 7 modules, which is 0.35 of the column and NOT the one third of Vignola's general rule. Esquie states the exception in as many words: 'rather more than one third the height of the column, and thus an exception to Vignola's general rule as to the height of pedestals.'
invariants.note: The one-third rule is Vignola's stated principle and it holds exactly in the Doric and the Ionic. It does not hold in the drawing here, and the drawing is what he built from. The 32-part division of the arcade-on-pedestals plate - 7 pedestal, 20 column, 5 entablature - is independent confirmation.

invariants.statement: The column is 20 modules, that is ten diameters.
Base, shaft and capital make the column: 1 + 16 2/3 + 2 1/3.
Architrave, frieze and cornice make the entablature.
The entablature divides in ten: three to the architrave, three to the frieze, four to the cornice (Esquie, plate XXX).
The capital is one diameter and one sixth - 2 modules 6 parts, the vase 2 modules and the abacus 6 parts.
The upper diameter is five sixths of the lower.
The shaft is cylindrical for its lower third and diminishes above.

named_spacings.name: pycnostyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian, not Vignola's. Vignola gives no named series; the names are carried here because American practice reads them onto him. Ware's American Vignola simplifies the series to 1, 2, 3 and 4 diameters clear.

named_spacings.name: eustyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian. This is the one Vignola's own Ionic colonnade lands on exactly.

named_spacings.name: araeostyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian; requires a timber architrave. Ware notes the ancients spaced Tuscan columns with wooden architraves as much as seven diameters apart.

named_spacings.name: vignola-corinthian-colonnade
named_spacings.note: Vignola's own: axes 6 2/3 modules = 3 1/3 diameters apart, so 2 1/3 diameters clear. It is not one of the Vitruvian five; it falls between eustyle and diastyle, and it is dictated by the cornice, not by taste. Modillions stand 2/3 D on centres, so 3 1/3 D is exactly five modillion spacings and one modillion lands on the axis of every column. Ware records that moderns prefer 2 1/3 diameters for exactly this reason.

named_spacings.name: vignola-corinthian-arcade
named_spacings.note: Arched: piers 3 modules, opening 9 modules wide by 18 high, axes 12 modules apart.

named_spacings.name: vignola-corinthian-arcade-on-pedestals
named_spacings.note: Arched on pedestals: axes 16 modules, piers 4 modules, opening 12 wide by 25 high; total height 32 modules, of which 7 pedestal, 20 column, 5 entablature. Vignola deliberately breaks his own 2:1 rule for the opening here - the extra module of height improves the bracket and deepens the keystone, and he says so.

derived_rules.note: A quarter of the column, base and capital included, at any scale. For the Corinthian this is the expensive rule: a ten-diameter column carries an entablature two and a half diameters deep, and the deeper the order the more of it is carved.

The room read as an order; the crown is the cornice member, 4 of the 10 parts of the Corinthian entablature. At a 10 ft ceiling this gives 9.6 in - a modillion cornice, and the right one for a principal room.
derived_rules.authority_note: Esquie, plate XXX: the entablature divided in ten, four to the cornice.

derived_rules.note: Vignola gives the Corinthian cornice a projection of 2 modules 2 parts against a height of 2 modules - slightly MORE than its height, unlike the Ionic. The modillions are what push it out.

Modillions 2/3 D = 24 parts on centres, each 2/9 D wide (8 parts) with 4/9 D between - exactly twice their width. Four dentils to each modillion: one under every modillion and three between, at 6 parts on centres. This is the alignment rule that governs the whole bay.
derived_rules.authority_note: Ware, The American Vignola, on the Corinthian cornice.

derived_rules.note: Modillions per bay at Vignola's own spacing of 6 2/3 modules on centres: five, with one on the axis of each column. Any bay that is not a whole multiple of 2/3 diameter will put a partial modillion somewhere, and there is nowhere good to put it.
derived_rules.authority_note: Esquie, plate XXVI: the axes 6 2/3 modules apart 'allows a modillion in the cornice always to be placed over the axis of a column.'

derived_rules.note: Of ceiling_height. Slightly heavier than the Ionic room takes, because the cornice above it is heavier and the two have to balance. The logic is still the plinth of the order.
derived_rules.authority_note: No classical source dimensions an interior baseboard; the band is honest.

derived_rules.note: Of the floor-to-cornice height. The chair rail is the cap of the pedestal at room scale, and in the Corinthian the pedestal is 7 of the 32 modules of the whole order - 0.219, about 26 in at a 10 ft ceiling. Note that Vignola's Corinthian pedestal is the tall one, so the Corinthian room legitimately carries a higher dado than the Ionic room. It is still below the 32 to 36 in that furniture wants.
derived_rules.authority_note: Vignola, Regola plate XXVIII: of 32 parts, 7 pedestal, 20 column, 5 entablature.

derived_rules.note: Of the floor-to-cornice height. The dado of the Corinthian room is the pedestal: die two squares high, cap 1/9 of the pedestal, base 1/10.5. Where the rail is raised to meet furniture the die must be restretched, not the cap.

Of opening_width, modelled on the architrave: three fascias and a large cymatium, the cymatium as high as the first fascia, the two lower fascias taking the lower half. In an 18-part casing that is 4 : 4 : 5 : 4 plus small mouldings - and the fascias must step forward as they rise or the casing reads flat.

Entablature over the door: the opening twice as high as wide, the entablature a quarter of the door height. Vignola's own Corinthian doorway, at SS. Lorenzo e Damaso, has brackets under the cornice that both ornament and carry it.
derived_rules.authority_note: Vignola, Regola, plate XXXI in the 1889 translation.

derived_rules.note: Of opening_width. Lighter than the door surround, because in a Corinthian elevation the windows are numerous and the entry must still win. Retargeted at ontology 0.3.0: 'window_surround' was split by trade, and this rule belongs to window_surround_wood. The other heir needs its own rule and does not yet have one.

Envelope cornice at building scale. On a 12 ft principal storey this is a 14.4 in cornice projecting 15.2 in, carried on modillions 8 in wide at 16 in on centres. That is a real cornice and it needs real framing; if the budget cannot carry it, the honest move is to change order, not to shrink the cornice.
Envelope frieze, 3 of the 10 parts. The Corinthian frieze is the natural place for a carved or pulvinated band; left plain it is simply the deepest board on the building.

A pilaster of the order is one lower diameter wide and carries the same capital, entablature and diminution as the column. Vignola's arcade piers are 3 modules and the column is engaged into them - a pilaster that is not the width of the column it stands for is a panel, not a pilaster.

conflicts.statement: Two tiers of eight acanthus leaves, eight caulicoli each dividing into an angle volute and a helix, sixteen leaves of a third row sheathing the caulicoli, and a rosette in each face of the abacus. Hand-carved in limewood this is weeks per capital; in stone it is months. It is the single most expensive element in classical building and no amount of good intention changes that.
conflicts.resolution: The honest substitutions, in descending order of honesty: (1) cast plaster or composition capitals from a good mould, painted - this is what most Georgian and Federal interiors actually had, and nobody has ever objected; (2) GFRC or cast stone outside, which takes the profile well and the weather better than wood; (3) a modelled but unsharpened leaf, which reads correctly at 20 ft and costs a third; (4) drop to the Composite, whose capital reads richer from below for the same money because the volutes do the work the acanthus would have done. What is NOT an honest substitution is a Corinthian capital with a single tier of leaves or with the caulicoli omitted - that is a different and worse capital wearing the name.

conflicts.statement: Modillion spacing at 2/3 diameter puts a bracket every 16 in on a 12 ft storey, each with a caissoned soffit panel and a rosette between. The soffit ornament alone can exceed the cost of the cornice framing.
conflicts.resolution: Run the modillions and leave the caissons plain, or coffer them without rosettes. Ware's own plate shows the caisson and rosette as the full treatment; Vignola's Roman sources vary. Omitting the rosette is a documented reduction. Omitting the modillions is not - it makes the cornice Composite, and the Composite is a different order with a different capital.

conflicts.statement: Modillions must fall at 2/3 diameter on centres with one on the axis of every column, which fixes the bay at a multiple of 2/3 D - Vignola's own bay is exactly five spacings. Contemporary window rhythm is set by code-minimum glazing area (IRC natural light at 8 per cent of floor area, ventilation at 4 per cent) and by stock sash sizes, neither of which knows anything about 2/3 of a diameter. The two grids will not agree, and the modillion grid is the one that shows.
conflicts.resolution: Set the module FROM the bay, not the bay from the module: choose the module so that the required bay is a whole multiple of 2/3 D, then let the column diameter follow. If the bay cannot be moved, take the licence Vignola himself provides and use the Composite denticular cornice, whose dentils Esquie says explicitly 'may be set out regardless of the axes of the columns'. Sliding the modillions to fit and letting one land off-axis is the wrong answer and is visible from the street.

conflicts.statement: At a 6 in module one part is 1/3 in. The fillets in the Corinthian cornice - 0.3 parts over the modillion band, 0.5 parts in the bed mould, 0.6 parts over the corona - are 0.1 to 0.2 in. They cannot be cut, cannot be painted, and cannot be inspected.
conflicts.resolution: This order does not work below about a 9 in module (18 in column) in painted wood. Above that, hold a 1/2 in minimum on every fillet and absorb the difference in the corona. If the design demands a small Corinthian, run it in plaster or cast it - cast members hold a 1/4 in fillet that millwork cannot.

conflicts.statement: Vignola's Corinthian doorway is twice as high as wide with an entablature a quarter of the door height. At a 36 in clear-width accessible door, that is a 72 in leaf and an 18 in entablature - a 90 in assembly. In an 8 ft ceiling there is 6 in left for the crown, and the crown wants 9.6.
conflicts.resolution: Either raise the ceiling to 9 ft 6 in, which is what the order assumes, or break the classical relation deliberately: keep the 1/6 casing, drop the full entablature to a simple crowned cap, and record the departure. Do not compress the entablature proportionally - a quarter-scale Corinthian entablature 6 in deep is unreadable and looks like a mistake rather than a decision.

Pierre Esquie, The Five Orders of Architecture according to Vignola, 1930 (archive.org/details/pierreesuie) - plates XVIII-XXXIX
William R. Ware, The American Vignola, part I: The Five Orders, 1902/1920 (archive.org/details/americanvignola01wareuoft; en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Ware_-_The_American_Vignola,_1920.djvu)

notes:
SKELETON, AND ITS AUTHORITY. Column 20 modules (ten diameters), entablature 5 modules, pedestal 7 modules. Base 1 module, shaft 16 modules 12 parts, capital 2 modules 6 parts, which sum to 20 exactly. Architrave 1 1/2 modules, frieze 1 1/2, cornice 2, which sum to 5 exactly and stand as 3 : 3 : 4. All of these are Vignola's own figures from the Regola, given in the 1889 translation (plates XX-XXV) and in Esquie (plates XXVI-XXXI), and confirmed by Ware's independent statement in diameters: base 1/2 D, capital 7/6 D, architrave 3/4 D, frieze 3/4 D, cornice 1 D.

THE CAPITAL AT ONE DIAMETER AND ONE SIXTH - VERIFIED. Vignola: 'this Capital 2 moduli and 6 parti, the vase being 2 moduli and the abacus 6 parti.' 42 parts = 7/6 of 36 = 1 1/6 D. Ware, independently: 'seven-sixths of a Diameter high, the upper sixth being taken up by the Abacus.' The bell divides into three equal sixths of a diameter - lower leaves, upper leaves, caulicoli - which is how the 12 : 12 : 12 : 6 encoded here is arrived at. The bell is cylindrical for its lower 1 module 10 parts and springs from a diameter of 5/6 D at the lip, which is a beak moulding 1/18 to 1/12 D thick.

THE MODILLION AND THE DENTIL BELOW IT. This is the relation the order is really about. The modillion is 5/12 D long - which is to say exactly half the upper diameter of the shaft - 1/5 D high, and as wide as one dentil plus two interdentils, 2/9 D. Modillions stand 2/3 D on centres with 4/9 D between them, exactly twice their width. Dentils stand 1/6 D on centres, so there are FOUR dentils to every modillion: one directly under each modillion and three between. Get that count wrong and the cornice is wrong no matter how well the pieces are cut. The whole intercolumniation follows from it: 6 2/3 modules between axes is five modillion spacings, and it exists so that a modillion can sit on the axis of every column. Ware records that where the ancients preferred 2 1/2 diameters clear, the moderns prefer 2 1/3 - and 2 1/3 is precisely Vignola's figure, arrived at from the cornice rather than from the eye.

THE PEDESTAL EXCEPTION - A CORRECTION TO THE GENERAL RULE. Vignola states in the Tuscan plate that 'in all the orders we have the general rule that the pedestal is one third part of the combined height', and that rule holds exactly in the Doric (5 1/3 to 16) and the Ionic (6 to 18). It does NOT hold here. Vignola draws the Corinthian pedestal at 7 modules against a column of 20, which is 0.35, and Esquie flags it: 'rather more than one third the height of the column, and thus an exception to Vignola's general rule as to the height of pedestals.' The 1889 translation says the same more gently - 'a little more than one third' - and the arcade-on-pedestals plate confirms it arithmetically by dividing the whole into 32 parts, 7 for the pedestal. Anyone who encodes 1/3 here is encoding the principle instead of the drawing. The die is two squares high, 100 parts by 50; its plinth is 4 parts and Esquie notes it may be increased to 8.

WHAT IS SOFT. The individual mouldings of the cornice. Ware's rule - the cornice divided into five equal parts, the two lower resembling the lower half of the Ionic cornice, the middle fifth the modillion band, the two upper the corona and cymatium - is the anchor, and the members encoded here sum to those fifths exactly (14.4, 7.2, 14.4 parts). The split within each fifth is a reconstruction at quarter-part precision; Vignola's plate carries the individual figures as drawn annotations that no consulted transcription reproduces. Those members are medium. Same for the architrave, where the group totals (6 + 6 + 1.5 below, 7.5 + 6 above, cymatium equal to the first fascia) are Ware's and the internal split is not. Ware himself warns that 'these dimensions and proportions vary greatly in different ancient examples and almost as much in modern ones.'

THE BASE. Encoded as the Attic base, as for the Ionic. Esquie: 'the base of the column is according to Vignola, but the Attic base was frequently used in Roman examples.' The 18-part total and the 6-part plinth are firm; the twelve parts between are the Attic construction and are marked medium.

PROJECTION DATUM. For the pedestal, base, shaft and capital assemblies, projection_parts is the HALF-WIDTH measured from the axis of the column; the naked of the shaft at its lower diameter is therefore 18 parts and the naked at its upper diameter 15 parts. For the architrave, frieze and cornice, projection_parts is measured from the NAKED OF THE FRIEZE, which stands 15 parts from the axis - Ware: 'the lower band of the Architrave is made to come in line with the upper face of the shaft.' The two conventions are the ones the sources themselves use and the schema anticipates both. Cross-check: Vignola gives the column base a projection of 7 parts from the side of the column (18+7 = 25) and the pedestal die a width of 2 modules 14 parts (half-width 25). The base sits exactly on the die. The arithmetic closes, which is how we know the datum is read right.
